questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A capacitor holds a charge of 240 μC when a potential difference of 60 V is applied across it. If the potential difference is raised to 90 V, the charge it holds becomes:

solution.concept: Capacitance C = Q/V is fixed by the geometry and the medium, so Q is proportional to V
solution.explanation: The capacitance found from the first reading stays the same when the voltage changes; only the charge changes.
steps: New charge Q = CV = 4 μF × 90 V = 360 μC
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 μC scales the charge by 60/90 instead of 90/60. 240 μC assumes the charge stays fixed. 540 μC scales the charge with V², which is how the stored energy (not the charge) changes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', capacitors and capacitance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Ten identical capacitors are first connected all in parallel and then all in series. The ratio of the equivalent capacitance of the parallel combination to that of the series combination is:

solution.concept: Parallel: C_p = sum of capacitances; series: 1/C_s = sum of reciprocals
solution.explanation: For n identical capacitors C, the parallel combination is nC and the series combination is C/n.
solution.shortcut: For n identical capacitors the ratio is n².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/100 is the series-to-parallel ratio, inverted. 10 compares only one of the combinations with a single capacitor. 1 assumes the arrangement does not matter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A student applies Gauss's law to a system of discrete point charges. Which of the following is a correct guideline for choosing the Gaussian surface?

options.text: It must be a sphere centred on one of the charges
It must be the surface of a real conductor
It must not pass through any of the discrete point charges
It must enclose all the charges, because charges outside change the total flux through it

solution.concept: Gauss's law and the Gaussian surface
solution.explanation: Any closed surface may be used as a Gaussian surface, of any shape or size, real or imaginary. The one caution NCERT gives is that the surface should not pass through a discrete charge, because the electric field of a system of point charges is not well defined at the location of a charge.
steps: Field undefined at a point charge → surface must not pass through one
solution.why_others_wrong: The sphere is only a convenient choice when there is spherical symmetry; Gauss's law holds for any shape. The surface may be imaginary. Charges outside the surface contribute zero total flux (they change the field on the surface, but not the net flux).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Gauss's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: It must not pass through any of the discrete point charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): To find the electric field produced by a source charge, the force is measured on a test charge that is made vanishingly small.
Reason (R): A test charge that is not small could push or pull the source charges and disturb their arrangement, so the field measured would not be the field of the original arrangement.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Definition of the electric field using a test charge
solution.explanation: The field at a point is E = F/q for a test charge q placed there. If q were large, the force it exerts on the source charges could move them (or, on a conductor, redistribute them), so the field being measured would be changed by the act of measuring it. Making q negligibly small avoids this. R is exactly why A is done.
steps: A: test charge made vanishingly small → true
R: a large test charge disturbs the source arrangement → true
R gives the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not an unrelated fact: it is the very reason the test charge must be small, so the 'NOT the correct explanation' option fails.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric field
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electron moves from a point where the electrostatic potential is 20 V to a point where it is 70 V. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the work done on the electron by the electric field is:

solution.concept: Work done by the field = −(change in potential energy) = −q(V_final − V_initial)
solution.explanation: The potential energy of a charge q at potential V is qV. For the electron q = −e, so moving to a higher potential lowers its potential energy, and the field does positive work on it.
solution.shortcut: A negative charge moving towards higher potential gains kinetic energy: |W| = e × 50 V = 50 eV, positive.
solution.why_others_wrong: −8.0 × 10⁻¹⁸ J treats the electron as a positive charge (or gives the work of an external agent). +1.12 × 10⁻¹⁷ J uses the final potential (70 V) alone. +1.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ J adds the two potentials instead of taking their difference.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a charge in an external field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Point charges, each of +2 μC, are placed at five of the six corners of a regular hexagon of side 30 cm, in air; the sixth corner is empty. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric field at the centre of the hexagon is:

options.text: 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed towards the empty corner
2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed away from the empty corner
1 × 10⁶ N/C, directed towards the empty corner

solution.concept: Superposition principle; symmetry
solution.explanation: If all six corners carried +2 μC, the fields at the centre would cancel in pairs (opposite corners). So the field of the five charges equals minus the field that the missing sixth charge would produce. A +2 μC charge at the empty corner would give a field at the centre pointing away from that corner; the actual field therefore points towards the empty corner. In a regular hexagon each corner is at a distance equal to the side from the centre.
steps: Distance of each corner from the centre = side = 0.30 m
Field of one charge there = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.09 = 2 × 10⁵ N/C
Five charges = six charges (zero) − one charge → 2 × 10⁵ N/C towards the empty corner
solution.shortcut: Field of the gap = field of a −2 μC charge placed at the empty corner.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Away from the empty corner' gets the magnitude right but reverses the direction. 1 × 10⁶ N/C adds the five magnitudes as if all the fields were parallel. Zero assumes the five charges are still symmetric.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 2 × 10⁵ N/C, directed towards the empty corner

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two protons are a distance r apart in vacuum. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and the proton mass as 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, the ratio of the electrostatic force between them to the gravitational force between them is about:

options.text: 1.2 × 10³⁶ at r = 1 m, and larger at smaller r

solution.concept: Coulomb's law and Newton's law of gravitation are both inverse-square laws
solution.explanation: Both forces vary as 1/r², so r cancels in the ratio: F_e/F_G = ke²/(Gm²).
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.1 × 10⁻³⁷ is the gravitational-to-electrostatic ratio. 2.1 × 10⁹ forgets to square the mass. The last option wrongly makes the ratio depend on r, although both forces fall off as 1/r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Coulomb's law
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.2 × 10³⁶, whatever the value of r

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An isolated parallel plate capacitor carries charges +40 μC and −40 μC on its plates. A slab of dielectric constant 5 is slid in so that it completely fills the space between the plates. The magnitude of the charge induced (by polarisation) on each face of the slab is:

solution.concept: Polarisation of a dielectric: induced surface charge reduces the field to E₀/K
solution.explanation: The free charge Q on the plates stays 40 μC (the capacitor is isolated). The face of the slab next to the positive plate acquires a charge −Q_p and the other face +Q_p. The field inside the slab is due to the net charge Q − Q_p, and it must be 1/K of the field without the slab.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 μC is Q/K, the net (free minus induced) charge, not the induced charge. 200 μC multiplies by K; the induced charge can never exceed the free charge. 40 μC would cancel the field inside completely, which happens in a conductor, not a dielectric.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', dielectrics and polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 20 pF parallel plate capacitor with air between its plates is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. Its plates are now slowly pulled apart until their separation is doubled. The work done by the agent pulling the plates apart is:

solution.concept: With the battery disconnected the charge stays constant; U = Q²/(2C)
solution.explanation: Doubling the separation halves the capacitance. With Q fixed, the stored energy Q²/(2C) doubles. The plates attract each other, so the agent does positive work, equal to the increase in stored energy.
steps: Initial energy U = ½CV² = ½ × 20 × 10⁻¹² × 100² = 1 × 10⁻⁷ J
C → C/2 with Q fixed → U → 2U = 2 × 10⁻⁷ J
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁷ J is the final stored energy, not the increase. −5 × 10⁻⁸ J treats the voltage as fixed (as if the battery stayed connected), which would halve the energy. The work is not zero: the attracting plates must be pulled apart.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (its dimensional formula). A stands for the dimension of electric current.

List-I:
A. Electric field
B. Electric potential
C. Capacitance
D. Permittivity of free space, ε₀

List-II:
I. [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²]
II. [M L T⁻³ A⁻¹]
III. [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]
IV. [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensions from defining relations: E = F/q, V = W/q, C = Q/V, ε₀ = C d/A
solution.explanation: Charge has dimensions [A T]. E = F/q = [M L T⁻²]/[A T] = [M L T⁻³ A⁻¹]. V = W/q = [M L² T⁻²]/[A T] = [M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹]. C = Q/V = [A T]/[M L² T⁻³ A⁻¹] = [M⁻¹ L⁻² T⁴ A²]. ε₀ = Cd/A has one more L⁻¹ than C: [M⁻¹ L⁻³ T⁴ A²] (its unit is F/m).
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping E and V confuses N/C with J/C (they differ by one power of length). Swapping C and ε₀ forgets that ε₀ is capacitance per unit length (F/m).
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two large, thin, parallel plane sheets carry the same uniform surface charge density +σ. In the region between the sheets (away from the edges), the electric field is zero.
Statement II: For the same two sheets, the electric field in the region outside them (away from the edges) has magnitude σ/(2ε₀).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Field of a large plane sheet, σ/(2ε₀), and superposition
solution.explanation: Each sheet produces a field of magnitude σ/(2ε₀) directed away from it on both sides. Between the sheets the two fields are opposite and cancel, so Statement I is true. Outside, both fields point the same way and add to σ/ε₀, so Statement II is false.
steps: Outside: σ/(2ε₀) + σ/(2ε₀) = σ/ε₀ → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: σ/(2ε₀) is the field of a single sheet; outside two like sheets the fields add.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', applications of Gauss's law: field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
An electric dipole of dipole moment p is placed in a non-uniform electric field E. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In general, the dipole experiences both a net force and a torque.
(b) If p is parallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of increasing field.
(c) If p is antiparallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of decreasing field.
(d) If p is parallel to E, the torque on the dipole is maximum.
(e) If p is antiparallel to E, the torque on the dipole is maximum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dipole in a non-uniform field: torque p × E and a net force that depends on how E varies
solution.explanation: In a non-uniform field the forces qE on the two charges are unequal, so there is in general a net force as well as a torque. With p parallel to E the dipole is pulled towards the stronger field; with p antiparallel it is pushed towards the weaker field (NCERT states both). The torque p × E has magnitude pE sin θ, which is zero (not maximum) when p is parallel or antiparallel to E.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (d) or (e) treats the aligned positions as positions of maximum torque; the torque is maximum when p is perpendicular to E.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', dipole in a uniform external field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two point charges, each of +8 μC, are fixed at x = 0 and x = 2a on the x-axis. A third point charge q is placed at x = a. For all three charges to be in equilibrium under their mutual electrostatic forces alone, q must be:

solution.concept: Equilibrium of a system of charges: net Coulomb force on each charge zero
solution.explanation: The middle charge is in equilibrium for any q, by symmetry. For the charge at x = 0, the repulsion from the other +8 μC charge (distance 2a) must be balanced by an attraction towards the middle charge (distance a), so q must be negative.
steps: Force on the end charge from the other end: k(8)(8)/(2a)² = 16k/a² (away)
Force from q: k(8)|q|/a² (towards q, if q is negative)
solution.shortcut: q = −Q/4 for equal charges Q at the ends.
solution.why_others_wrong: +2 μC has the right size but would repel the end charges. −8 μC ignores that the middle charge is at half the distance. −4 μC uses distances a and 2a without squaring them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', forces between multiple charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A total charge of 5 nC is shared between two thin concentric conducting spherical shells of radii 10 cm and 20 cm (kept insulated from each other) so that the two shells have equal surface charge densities. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the electric potential at the common centre is:

solution.concept: Potential due to a charged spherical shell; superposition of potentials
solution.explanation: Equal surface densities mean the charges are in the ratio of the areas, r₁² : r₂² = 1 : 4, so the shells carry 1 nC and 4 nC. Inside a shell its potential is constant and equal to kQ/R, so at the centre each shell contributes kQ/R.
steps: Q₁ : Q₂ = 10² : 20² = 1 : 4 → Q₁ = 1 nC, Q₂ = 4 nC
solution.why_others_wrong: 450 V puts the whole 5 nC on the inner shell. 405 V divides the charge in the inverse ratio (4 nC on the inner shell). 225 V puts all the charge on the outer shell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential due to a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 5 μF capacitor charged to 200 V is disconnected from the battery and connected across an uncharged capacitor of unknown capacitance. The common potential difference across the two capacitors settles at 40 V. The energy dissipated (as heat and radiation) during the redistribution of charge is:

solution.concept: Conservation of charge when capacitors are connected; stored energy ½CV²
solution.explanation: Charge is conserved: 5 μF × 200 V = 1000 μC is shared between the two capacitors at 40 V, so the total capacitance is 25 μF and the unknown capacitor is 20 μF. The energy lost is the initial stored energy minus the final stored energy.
steps: Q = 5 μF × 200 V = 1000 μC; total C = 1000/40 = 25 μF → unknown C = 20 μF
solution.shortcut: Loss = ½ [C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂)] V₁² = ½ × 4 μF × (200 V)² = 0.08 J.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.02 J is the energy finally stored. 0.1 J is the energy initially stored. 0.016 J is the energy finally stored in the 20 μF capacitor alone.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a dielectric slab that completely fills the space between the plates is inserted into an air-filled parallel plate capacitor that remains connected to a battery, the electric field between the plates does not change.
Reason (R): With the battery connected, the potential difference V between the plates and the plate separation d both stay the same, and the uniform field between the plates is E = V/d.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Capacitor with a dielectric: which quantity is held fixed
solution.explanation: The familiar result that a dielectric reduces the field to E₀/K applies when the charge is fixed (isolated capacitor). With the battery connected, V is fixed; the field in the filled gap is V/d, so it cannot change. The battery supplies extra charge (K times the original) so that the field of the free charges, reduced by the polarisation charges, is again V/d. R states exactly why A holds.
steps: A: V fixed, d fixed → E = V/d unchanged → true
R: true, and it is the reason for A
solution.why_others_wrong: Students who apply E₀/K regardless of the battery would mark A false; that rule needs the charge to be fixed. R is not an unrelated fact; it is the derivation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', effect of dielectric on capacitance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 50 μF capacitor already charged to 4 V is connected, through a resistor and with like terminals joined, to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance, and is left until it is fully charged to 12 V. The heat produced in the resistor during this process is:

solution.concept: Energy balance in charging: work done by the battery = increase in stored energy + heat
solution.explanation: The battery moves the extra charge ΔQ = C(12 − 4) through its emf of 12 V, so it does work ΔQ × 12 V. Only part of this goes into the capacitor's stored energy; the rest is dissipated in the resistor.
steps: ΔQ = 50 μF × 8 V = 400 μC; battery work = 400 μC × 12 V = 4.8 mJ
Increase in stored energy = ½ × 50 μF × (12² − 4²) V² = 3.2 mJ
solution.shortcut: Heat = ½C(ΔV)² = ½ × 50 μF × 8² = 1.6 mJ when a battery tops up a capacitor through a resistor.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.2 mJ is the increase in stored energy. 4.8 mJ is the work done by the battery. 2.4 mJ assumes that half of the battery's work always becomes heat, which is true only when the capacitor starts uncharged.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electric bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V. Treating its resistance as constant, the resistance of its filament when it is working at its rated voltage is:

solution.concept: Electrical power P = V²/R
solution.explanation: At its rated voltage the bulb draws its rated power, so R = V²/P.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.2 Ω is V/P, which has no physical meaning here. 0.45 is P/V, the current in amperes, not a resistance. 22 kΩ multiplies V by P.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A current of 6 A enters a parallel combination of a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. The current through the 4 Ω resistor is:

solution.concept: In a parallel combination the potential difference is the same, so the current divides in inverse proportion to the resistances
solution.explanation: The equivalent resistance is 2 × 4/(2 + 4) = 4/3 Ω, so the common potential difference is 6 A × 4/3 Ω = 8 V.
steps: Current in 4 Ω = 8/4 = 2 A (and 4 A in the 2 Ω resistor)
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 A is the current in the 2 Ω resistor (the larger share goes through the smaller resistance). 3 A assumes an equal split. 6 A treats the resistors as if they were in series.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current through a metal wire is doubled, and at the same time the wire is replaced by another wire of the same metal (at the same temperature) with half the cross-sectional area. The drift speed of the free electrons becomes:

solution.concept: I = n e A v_d, so v_d = I/(n e A)
solution.explanation: The number density n of free electrons is a property of the metal and does not change. The drift speed is proportional to I and inversely proportional to A.
solution.why_others_wrong: '2 times' accounts for the doubled current but not the smaller area. 'The same' assumes the two changes cancel. '1/4' inverts the dependence on both I and A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: 4 times the original value

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Although the drift speed of the free electrons in a copper wire is only of the order of 1 mm/s, a wire of cross-sectional area 1 mm² can carry a current of several amperes.
Reason (R): The number density of free electrons in a metal such as copper is very large, of the order of 10²⁸ to 10²⁹ per cubic metre.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Current in terms of drift speed: I = n e A v_d
solution.explanation: The current through a cross-section is the charge carried across it per second, n e A v_d. With n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, A = 10⁻⁶ m² and v_d = 10⁻³ m/s, I ≈ 14 A. A tiny drift speed still gives a sizeable current only because n is enormous, so R explains A.
steps: I = n e A v_d: small v_d is compensated by very large n → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate property: the large n is exactly what makes the current large in spite of the small drift speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The resistivity of a metal wire at a given temperature increases if the wire is made longer.
Statement II: The SI unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance, is the siemens (S), with 1 S = 1 Ω⁻¹.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Resistance depends on dimensions; resistivity is a property of the material
solution.explanation: R = ρl/A depends on the length and area, but ρ depends only on the material and its temperature, so Statement I is false. Conductance G = 1/R is measured in siemens, 1 S = 1 Ω⁻¹, so Statement II is true.
steps: I: a longer wire has more resistance, not more resistivity → false
II: G = 1/R, unit S = Ω⁻¹ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses resistance with resistivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three identical bulbs, connected in series across a supply of constant voltage, together consume a power P. Treating the resistance of each bulb as constant, the total power they consume when they are connected in parallel across the same supply is:

solution.concept: For a fixed supply voltage, total power = V²/R_eq
solution.explanation: In series the equivalent resistance is 3R; in parallel it is R/3, which is 9 times smaller. With V fixed, power is inversely proportional to the equivalent resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3P compares the parallel combination with a single bulb's resistance R. P/9 inverts the ratio. P assumes the arrangement does not matter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 18 Ω is bent into the shape of an equilateral triangle ABC, its ends being joined. The resistance between the corner A and the midpoint M of the opposite side BC is:

solution.concept: Resistance proportional to length; parallel combination
solution.explanation: Each side is 6 Ω, and half a side is 3 Ω. From A to M there are two identical paths: A → B → M and A → C → M, each of 6 + 3 = 9 Ω. These two paths are in parallel.
steps: Each side 6 Ω; BM = MC = 3 Ω
Each path A→B→M or A→C→M = 9 Ω
Two 9 Ω paths in parallel = 4.5 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 Ω takes only one of the two paths. 4 Ω is the resistance between two corners (6 Ω in parallel with 12 Ω). 6 Ω is just the resistance of one side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two wires X and Y are made of the same metal and have the same mass. The length of Y is twice that of X. The two wires are connected in series across a battery. The ratio of the heat produced per second in X to that in Y is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A, with equal mass (equal volume) fixing A = volume/l; in series, heat ∝ R
solution.explanation: Same metal and same mass means the same volume V. The cross-sectional area is A = V/l, so R = ρl/A = ρl²/V, i.e. R ∝ l². In series the same current flows through both, so the heat per second I²R is proportional to R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 uses R ∝ l and forgets that the longer wire is also thinner. 4 : 1 is the ratio for a parallel connection, where heat ∝ 1/R. 1 : 8 cubes the length ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials; electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A cell has emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. Match each situation in List-I with the potential difference between the terminals of the cell in List-II.

List-I:
A. No current is drawn from the cell (open circuit)
B. The terminals are joined directly by a thick wire of negligible resistance
C. A 2 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals
D. The cell is being charged by an external source, the charging current being 2 A

List-II:
I. 8 V
II. 0 V
III. 6 V
IV. 4 V

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Terminal potential difference V = ε − Ir while discharging and V = ε + Ir while charging
solution.explanation: Open circuit: no current, so V = ε = 6 V. Short circuit: the terminals are at the same potential, V = 0 (the current ε/r = 6 A makes Ir = ε). With 2 Ω: I = 6/3 = 2 A and V = 6 − 2 × 1 = 4 V. While charging, the current enters the positive terminal and V = ε + Ir = 6 + 2 = 8 V.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes either give the charging case ε − Ir (4 V), or give the short-circuited cell its emf, although its terminals are joined by a wire of negligible resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 4 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of a 6 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor, and the arrangement is connected across a battery. In which resistor is heat produced at the greatest rate?

options.text: The 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors equally, since they have the same potential difference

solution.concept: Heat produced per second = I²R; current division in a parallel combination
solution.explanation: Let the current through the 4 Ω resistor be I. It divides in inverse ratio of the resistances: 2I/3 through 6 Ω and I/3 through 12 Ω. The heating rates are 4I², 6(2I/3)² = 8I²/3 and 12(I/3)² = 4I²/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: The 6 Ω resistor gets more heat than the 12 Ω one (same V, so heat ∝ 1/R), but still less than the 4 Ω resistor, which carries the full current. The 12 Ω resistor gets the least. Equal potential difference does not mean equal heat when the resistances differ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy, power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A voltmeter of very high resistance connected directly across the terminals of a cell reads very nearly the emf of the cell.
Reason (R): Such a voltmeter draws a negligible current, so the potential drop across the internal resistance of the cell is negligible.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: The terminal voltage differs from the emf by the drop Ir across the internal resistance. A voltmeter of very high resistance R_V draws a current ε/(R_V + r), which is tiny, so Ir is tiny and the reading is almost ε. R gives the reason for A.
steps: I ≈ 0 for a very high resistance voltmeter → V ≈ ε
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the direct reason for A; it is not an unrelated statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The resistance of a metal wire is 50 Ω at 0 °C and 70 Ω at 100 °C. Assuming that the resistance varies linearly with temperature, the temperature at which its resistance is 61 Ω is:

solution.concept: R_t = R₀(1 + αt) for a linear variation
solution.explanation: The resistance rises by 20 Ω over 100 °C, i.e. 0.2 Ω per °C. A rise of 11 Ω above the 0 °C value therefore needs 55 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 87 °C takes R/R₁₀₀ × 100. 122 °C takes R/R₀ × 100. 45 °C measures the 11 Ω step down from 100 °C instead of up from 0 °C.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twelve identical resistors, each of 5 Ω, form a wheel: six of them make the sides of a regular hexagon (the rim) and the other six join each corner of the hexagon to its centre O (the spokes). The equivalent resistance between two diametrically opposite corners of the hexagon is:

solution.concept: Symmetry of a network and Kirchhoff's junction rule
solution.explanation: Hold corner 1 at potential V and the opposite corner 4 at 0. By symmetry the centre O is at V/2, corners 2 and 6 (next to 1) are at a common potential x, and corners 3 and 5 are at V − x. Apply the junction rule at corner 2, which is joined to 1, to 3 and to O.
steps: At corner 2: (V − x) + ((V − x) − x) + (V/2 − x) = 0 → x = 5V/8
Current leaving corner 1 (each resistor 5 Ω): [2(V − 5V/8) + (V − V/2)]/5 = (5V/4)/5 = V/4
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5 Ω uses only the two rim paths (15 Ω each, in parallel). 30/7 Ω adds the 10 Ω spoke path through O in parallel with the rim but ignores the spokes to the other corners, which carry current. 10 Ω uses the spoke path alone.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge with a 10 Ω standard resistor in the right gap, the null point is 50.0 cm from the left end when a resistor X is in the left gap, and 60.0 cm from the left end when X is replaced by a resistor Y. When X and Y are connected in parallel and placed together in the left gap (10 Ω still in the right gap), the null point will be at a distance from the left end of:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance: X/R = l/(100 − l)
solution.explanation: The two separate balances give X and Y; their parallel combination is then balanced against the same 10 Ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 71.4 cm uses X and Y in series (25 Ω). 55.0 cm simply averages the two balance lengths. 62.5 cm is the correct balance length measured from the wrong (right-hand) end.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 9 Ω is stretched uniformly to three times its original length, its volume and resistivity remaining unchanged. It is then cut into three pieces of equal length, and the three pieces are connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with volume constant gives R ∝ l²; identical resistors in parallel
solution.explanation: Stretching to three times the length at constant volume reduces the area to one third, so the resistance becomes 3² = 9 times larger. Each third of the stretched wire then has one third of that resistance, and three equal resistors in parallel give one third of one piece.
steps: Three 27 Ω pieces in parallel: 27/3 = 9 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 Ω ignores the stretching (pieces of 3 Ω in parallel). 27 Ω is the resistance of one piece. 3 Ω uses R ∝ l for the stretching, forgetting that the area also decreases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law; resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Wheatstone bridge, resistors P and Q form one branch and R and S the other; both branches are connected across a cell of emf ε and internal resistance r, and a galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. The bridge is balanced. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) No current flows through the galvanometer.
(b) The balance condition P/Q = R/S does not depend on the emf of the cell.
(c) The balance condition does not depend on the resistance of the galvanometer.
(d) The balance condition depends on the internal resistance of the cell.
(e) If the galvanometer is replaced by a resistor of any value, the currents through P, Q, R and S do not change.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Balanced Wheatstone bridge: the two junctions are at the same potential
solution.explanation: At balance the P–Q and R–S junctions are at the same potential, so no current flows through anything connected between them, whatever its resistance. Hence (a) and (e). The condition P/Q = R/S comes from the ratios of the resistances alone; ε, r and the galvanometer resistance change only the size of the currents, not whether the bridge balances. So (b) and (c) are true and (d) is false.
steps: (d) false: r affects the currents, not the balance
(e) true: no PD across the junctions, so no current in any element joining them
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) wrongly make the balance depend on the cell; the option without (e) misses that a balanced bridge passes no current between the junctions whatever element joins them; the option without (a) misses the defining property of balance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.25 Ω, are connected in series to form a closed ring (the positive terminal of each joined to the negative terminal of the next), with nothing else in the circuit. The current in the ring and the reading of an ideal voltmeter connected across the terminals of any one cell are, respectively:

solution.concept: Current in a closed loop of cells; terminal voltage V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: Round the ring the emfs add to 6 V and the internal resistances to 1 Ω, so the current is 6 A. For each cell the drop across its internal resistance is Ir = 6 × 0.25 = 1.5 V, exactly its emf, so its terminal voltage is zero.
steps: Total emf = 4 × 1.5 = 6 V; total resistance = 4 × 0.25 = 1 Ω
Terminal voltage of each cell = 1.5 − 6 × 0.25 = 0 V
solution.shortcut: By symmetry all four terminals of the ring must be at the same potential, so every voltmeter reads zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 V is the emf, which a voltmeter would read only if no current flowed. 24 A divides the total emf by the internal resistance of one cell. 'Zero' current wrongly assumes the cells cancel; they all push current the same way round the ring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: The magnetic susceptibility of a material is −2.0 × 10⁻⁵. Its relative magnetic permeability and the class of magnetic material it belongs to are:

solution.concept: Relative permeability μ_r = 1 + χ; a small negative χ (μ_r slightly less than 1) marks a diamagnetic material
solution.explanation: Susceptibility and relative permeability are related by μ_r = 1 + χ. A small negative susceptibility means the material is magnetised weakly opposite to the applied field, which is diamagnetism.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.00002 adds the magnitude of χ and would describe a paramagnetic material. −2.0 × 10⁻⁵ is χ itself, not μ_r. A paramagnetic material has μ_r slightly greater than 1.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A straight wire 20 cm long carries a current of 5 A in a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. As the orientation of the wire in the field is changed, the largest and the smallest possible magnitudes of the magnetic force on it are, respectively:

solution.concept: Force on a straight current-carrying conductor: F = I l B sin θ
solution.explanation: The force is largest when the wire is perpendicular to the field (sin θ = 1) and zero when the wire lies along the field (sin θ = 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.20 N is the force at 30° (sin 30° = ½); it is not a minimum. 40 N keeps the length in centimetres. 0.20 N as the maximum halves the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A ferromagnetic material consists of domains; a typical domain is about 1 mm across and contains about 10¹¹ atoms whose magnetic moments are aligned in the same direction.
Statement II: When a paramagnetic sample is kept in a fixed weak magnetic field and its temperature is raised, its magnetisation increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Domains in ferromagnets; effect of temperature on paramagnets
solution.explanation: Statement I is NCERT's description of domains. Statement II is false: in a paramagnet, thermal agitation randomises the atomic dipoles, so at higher temperature fewer of them line up with the field and the magnetisation decreases (Curie's law, M ∝ B/T).
steps: II: M ∝ 1/T for a paramagnet → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the effect of temperature on a paramagnet.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism; paramagnetism
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A square loop of wire lies in the x–y plane and carries a steady current that circulates anticlockwise when viewed from a point on the positive z-axis. The magnetic dipole moment of the loop is directed along:

options.text: the diagonal of the square, in the plane of the loop

solution.concept: Magnetic moment of a current loop: m = I A, with A along the normal given by the right-hand rule
solution.explanation: The magnetic moment is perpendicular to the plane of the loop. Curling the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current, the thumb points along m. An anticlockwise current seen from +z gives m along +z.
steps: Right-hand rule: anticlockwise seen from +z → m along +z
solution.why_others_wrong: −z would correspond to a clockwise current seen from +z. A magnetic moment never lies in the plane of a plane loop, so +x and the diagonal are both wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the current loop as a magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid becomes much stronger when a soft iron core is placed inside it.
Reason (R): Soft iron is ferromagnetic, with a relative permeability very much larger than 1, so it is strongly magnetised along the field of the solenoid.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Field in a solenoid filled with a material: B = μ₀μ_r n I
solution.explanation: With the core in place, the field is μ_r times the field of the empty solenoid. For soft iron μ_r is very large (its domains line up readily with the applied field), so the field increases greatly. R is the cause of A.
steps: Empty solenoid: B₀ = μ₀ n I
With core: B = μ_r B₀, μ_r ≫ 1 for soft iron
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate property of iron; the strong magnetisation of the core is exactly why the field grows.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', ferromagnetism
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: The magnetic field well inside a long, air-filled solenoid carrying a steady current is 2.5 mT. The solenoid is completely filled with a paramagnetic material of magnetic susceptibility 2.0 × 10⁻⁴, the current being kept the same. The magnetic field inside the solenoid:

solution.concept: Field in a material: B = µ₀µ_r H with µ_r = 1 + χ; a paramagnetic material has a small positive χ
solution.explanation: With the current unchanged, the field inside becomes µ_r = 1 + χ times the field of the empty solenoid. For a paramagnetic material χ is small and positive, so the field increases slightly; the increase is χ times the original field.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Decreases' is what a diamagnetic material (χ < 0) would do. 'Becomes 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ T' multiplies B₀ by χ instead of by 1 + χ, leaving almost no field. 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ T treats χ as a percentage (×100).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetisation and magnetic intensity; paramagnetism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 60 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 30 mA. It is converted into an ammeter of range 0–3 A by connecting a suitable shunt. The resistance of the ammeter so formed (galvanometer and shunt together) is:

solution.concept: Conversion of a galvanometer into an ammeter: a low resistance shunt S in parallel
solution.explanation: At full scale, 30 mA flows through the galvanometer and the remaining 2.97 A through the shunt, both having the same potential difference I_g G across them. The ammeter's resistance is the parallel combination of G and S, which is also (I_g G)/I.
steps: R_ammeter = G S/(G + S) = 1.8 V / 3 A = 0.60 Ω
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.606 Ω is the shunt alone. 60.6 Ω adds G and S as if they were in series. 60 Ω ignores the shunt.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (an SI unit in which it can be expressed).

List-I:
A. Magnetisation (magnetic moment per unit volume)
B. Magnetic susceptibility
C. Magnetic dipole moment
D. Current sensitivity of a moving-coil galvanometer

List-II:
I. A m⁻¹
II. no unit (a pure number)
III. J T⁻¹
IV. rad A⁻¹

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Units from definitions: M = m/V, χ = M/H, U = −m·B, current sensitivity φ/I
solution.explanation: Magnetisation is magnetic moment (A m²) per unit volume (m³): A m⁻¹. Susceptibility is the ratio of two quantities with the same unit (M and H), so it has none. From U = −m·B, m has the unit J T⁻¹ (equivalent to A m²). Current sensitivity is deflection per unit current: rad A⁻¹.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange magnetisation with magnetic moment (they differ by a factor of volume), or give susceptibility a unit although it is a ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetisation and magnetic intensity
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A small particle of mass 1.0 g carrying a charge of +1.0 μC is projected horizontally, at right angles to a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.50 T, in a direction such that the magnetic force on it is vertically upwards. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed with which it must be projected so that it moves along a horizontal straight line is:

solution.concept: Magnetic force qvB balancing the weight mg
solution.explanation: For straight-line motion the upward magnetic force must cancel the weight exactly. Since v is perpendicular to B, the force is qvB, and it stays vertical as long as the particle moves horizontally.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10³ m/s leaves out g. 2.0 × 10⁷ m/s keeps the mass in grams. 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/s inverts the expression.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
An electron (charge −e, mass mₑ) revolves with speed v in a circular orbit of radius r round the nucleus, as in the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom. Its orbital angular momentum is l. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The magnitude of its orbital magnetic moment is evr/2.
(b) The ratio of the magnitude of its orbital magnetic moment to that of its orbital angular momentum is e/(2mₑ).
(c) Its orbital magnetic moment points in the same direction as its orbital angular momentum.
(d) The smallest value of the orbital magnetic moment, the Bohr magneton, is about 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A m².
(e) The equivalent current of the revolving electron is ev/r.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Magnetic dipole moment of a revolving electron
solution.explanation: The revolving electron is a current loop with I = e/T = ev/(2πr), so μ = Iπr² = evr/2. Since l = mₑvr, μ/l = e/(2mₑ). Because the electron's charge is negative, its magnetic moment is opposite to its angular momentum: μ = −(e/2mₑ) l. Using Bohr's l = h/2π gives the least value eh/(4πmₑ) ≈ 9.27 × 10⁻²⁴ A m², the Bohr magneton.
steps: (c) false: opposite, as the charge is negative
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) forget the negative charge of the electron; options with (e) leave out the 2π in the period 2πr/v.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic dipole moment of a revolving electron

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A charged particle moving along a helix in a uniform magnetic field (no other force acting) has a constant velocity.
Statement II: The kinetic energy of such a particle remains constant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity: it changes direction, not speed
solution.explanation: The magnetic force q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: the speed and the kinetic energy stay constant (Statement II true). But the direction of motion keeps changing round the helix, so the velocity, a vector, is not constant (Statement I false).
steps: I: direction changes → velocity not constant → false
II: F ⊥ v → no work → KE constant → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I confuses constant speed with constant velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two identical circular loops of wire are placed coaxially, a short distance apart, in parallel planes. They carry steady currents circulating in the same sense when viewed along the common axis. The loops will:

options.text: exert no force on each other, since their fields are parallel
rotate so that their planes become perpendicular

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents; a current loop as a magnetic dipole
solution.explanation: Facing portions of the two loops carry currents in the same direction, and parallel currents in the same direction attract. Equivalently, each loop is a magnetic dipole and the two moments point the same way along the common axis, so the north face of one faces the south face of the other.
steps: Adjacent segments carry parallel currents → attraction
Dipole picture: moments aligned along the axis, N of one facing S of the other → attraction
solution.why_others_wrong: Repulsion would need opposite senses of circulation. The loops do exert forces on each other. Coaxial loops with aligned moments are already in equilibrium as far as torque is concerned, so they do not turn.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', force between two parallel currents; the current loop as a magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A thin flexible circular loop of wire of radius 10 cm lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T and carries a current of 4.0 A, in the sense for which the magnetic forces on it act outwards (away from its centre) everywhere. The tension in the wire is:

options.text: zero, because the net force on the loop is zero

solution.concept: Force on a curved conductor in a uniform field; equilibrium of half the loop
solution.explanation: Consider one half of the loop. The magnetic force on a semicircle in a uniform field equals the force on the straight diameter joining its ends: B I (2R), directed outwards. This half is held in equilibrium by the tension T acting at each of its two cut ends, both pulling towards the other half: 2T = 2BIR.
steps: Force on a semicircle = B I × 2R = 0.50 × 4.0 × 0.20 = 0.40 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.40 N is the net magnetic force on half the loop, which is shared by two ends. 1.3 N multiplies B I by the whole circumference, adding force magnitudes that point in different directions. The net force on the whole loop is zero, but each part is still stretched.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a steady current of 10 A. At an instant when a proton is 5.0 cm from the wire, it is moving with a speed of 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s directly towards the wire (along the perpendicular from it to the wire). Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the magnetic force on the proton at that instant is:

options.text: 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, parallel to the wire and in the direction of the current
1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, directed away from the wire
1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, parallel to the wire and opposite to the current
6.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ N, parallel to the wire and opposite to the current

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire; Lorentz force F = q v × B
solution.explanation: Take the wire along the z-axis with the current along +z, and the proton on the +x axis moving in the −x direction. At that point the field is along +y (right-hand rule). Then v × B = (−v x̂) × (B ŷ) = −vB ẑ, so the force is parallel to the wire and opposite to the current.
steps: Direction: (−x̂) × ŷ = −ẑ → opposite to the current
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In the direction of the current' reverses the cross product. 'Away from the wire' is the direction for a proton moving parallel to the current in the opposite direction, not one moving towards the wire. 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ N uses µ₀I/(4πd) for the field, half the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law (field of a straight wire); magnetic force
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, parallel to the wire and opposite to the current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 2.0 mA. It is made into a two-range voltmeter: a resistor R₁ in series with the galvanometer gives the 0–5 V range, and a further resistor R₂ added in series with R₁ (between R₁ and a second terminal) gives the 0–20 V range. The values of R₁ and R₂ are:

solution.concept: Galvanometer as a voltmeter: total resistance = range ÷ full-scale current
solution.explanation: On the 5 V range the total resistance must be 5/0.002 = 2500 Ω, which includes the 50 Ω galvanometer. On the 20 V range the total must be 20/0.002 = 10 000 Ω, which includes both the galvanometer and R₁.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2500 Ω and 10 000 Ω are the total resistances of the two ranges, not the added resistors. 9950 Ω is the resistor needed for 20 V on its own, forgetting that R₁ is already in the circuit. 2500 Ω for R₁ ignores the galvanometer's own resistance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
In a region there are a uniform electric field E and a uniform magnetic field B, both directed along the +z axis. A positively charged particle is introduced into the region (gravity negligible). Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If it is released from rest, it moves along a straight line parallel to the z-axis with uniform acceleration.
(b) If its initial velocity is perpendicular to the z-axis, it moves along a helix about an axis parallel to z, advancing a greater distance along z in each successive turn.
(c) Its speed remains constant whatever its initial velocity.
(d) The magnetic force on it does no work.
(e) The time it takes for each turn round the z-direction is 2πm/(qB), the same for every turn.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Superposition of the motions due to E and B when the fields are parallel
solution.explanation: The electric force qE is along z and changes only the z-component of velocity, uniformly. The magnetic force acts only on the velocity component perpendicular to B (which E does not change), giving uniform circular motion in the x–y projection with period 2πm/(qB). Released from rest, there is no perpendicular velocity and the particle simply accelerates along z. With a perpendicular initial velocity the path is a helix whose step along z grows each turn, because v_z keeps increasing. The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, but the electric force does work, so the speed is not constant.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) forget that the electric field does work on the charge; the options leaving out (b) or (e) miss that the circular part of the motion depends only on B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field; motion in combined electric and magnetic fields

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: An electron with a kinetic energy of 100 eV moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 1.0 mT (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Treating the circulating electron as a current loop, the magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment and its direction relative to the field are:

options.text: 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ A m², opposite to the field
1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ A m², opposite to the field
1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ A m², opposite to the field

solution.concept: Magnetic moment of a circulating charge, μ = IA with I = q/T; radius r = mv/(qB)
solution.explanation: For a charge circulating in a field B: I = e/T = e²B/(2πm) and A = πr² with r = mv/(eB). Then μ = IA = e²B r²/(2m) = (½mv²)/B, the kinetic energy divided by the field. The sense of circulation is such that the moment opposes the applied field (for either sign of charge), the same tendency that underlies diamagnetism.
steps: μ = evr/2 with r = mv/(eB) → μ = mv²/(2B) = KE/B
μ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ A m², opposite to B
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Along the field' gets the sense of circulation wrong: an electron in a field B along +z circulates anticlockwise seen from +z, so the conventional current is clockwise and the moment points along −z. 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ A m² uses mv²/B, dropping the ½. 1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ A m² multiplies KE by B instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field; magnetic dipole moment of a revolving electron
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ A m², opposite to the field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: When a steady current of 2.0 A flows through a coil, the energy stored in its magnetic field is 0.40 J. The self-inductance of the coil is:

solution.concept: Magnetic energy stored in an inductor: U = ½ L I²
solution.explanation: Rearranging U = ½LI² gives L = 2U/I².
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.10 H drops the factor ½ from U = ½LI². 0.40 H divides by I instead of I². 0.05 H puts the ½ on the wrong side of the equation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For a coil of self-inductance L and resistance R, the ratio L/R has the dimensions of:

solution.concept: Dimensional analysis using ε = L dI/dt and V = IR
solution.explanation: From ε = L (dI/dt), the unit of L is V s A⁻¹ = Ω s. Dividing by the unit of R (Ω) leaves seconds, so L/R has the dimensions of time. (It is the time constant of an L–R circuit.)
solution.why_others_wrong: Frequency would be R/L, the inverse. L/R is not a resistance and it is not dimensionless, since the henry is an ohm-second.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit is in resonance at a frequency f₀. Keeping L and R unchanged, the capacitance C must be changed to which value so that the resonant frequency becomes 2f₀?

solution.concept: Resonant frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC))
solution.explanation: The resonant frequency varies inversely as the square root of C. To double it with L fixed, √C must be halved, so C must become one quarter.
solution.why_others_wrong: C/2 treats f as inversely proportional to C, not to √C. 2C and 4C change C in the wrong direction; they would lower the resonant frequency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit: resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a pair of coils, the flux linked with the second coil per unit current in the first equals the flux linked with the first coil per unit current in the second; that is, M₁₂ = M₂₁.
Statement II: Self-inductance and mutual inductance are both measured in the same SI unit, the henry.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Mutual inductance and its unit
solution.explanation: NCERT shows for two long coaxial solenoids that M₁₂ = M₂₁ and states that the relation holds in general, so Statement I is true. Both inductances are flux linkage per unit current (Wb A⁻¹), the henry, so Statement II is true.
steps: II: unit of both = henry = Wb A⁻¹ → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true; neither is a trap.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', mutual inductance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A closed coil B (not connected to any battery) is placed close to a coil A, the two being coaxial. A steady battery is connected to A through a switch. When the switch is closed, coil B is:

options.text: attracted towards A, but only while the current in A is growing
repelled from A, but only while the current in A is growing
repelled from A for as long as the current in A flows
not acted on by any force, since no battery drives a current in B

solution.concept: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change of flux that produces it
solution.explanation: While the current in A grows, the flux through B increases, so the induced current in B circulates in the opposite sense to the current in A, opposing the increase. Antiparallel currents repel (equivalently, like poles face each other), so B is pushed away. Once the current in A is steady, the flux through B no longer changes, the induced current stops and so does the force.
steps: Growing current in A → increasing flux through B
Induced current in B opposite to that in A → repulsion
Steady current in A → no induced current → no force
solution.why_others_wrong: Attraction would occur while the current in A is decreasing (for example when the switch is opened). A steady current induces nothing, so the force does not last. B needs no battery: the changing flux induces a current in it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: repelled from A, but only while the current in A is growing

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The current in an ideal coil of self-inductance 0.50 H is increasing at a steady rate of 4.0 A/s. At the instant when the current is 2.0 A, the rate at which energy is being stored in the magnetic field of the coil is:

solution.concept: Energy stored U = ½LI², so dU/dt = L I (dI/dt) = (self-induced emf) × current
solution.explanation: The source must push the current against the self-induced emf L dI/dt = 0.50 × 4.0 = 2.0 V. The power it delivers to the coil, all of which is stored in the field of an ideal coil, is this emf times the current.
steps: dU/dt = emf × I = 2.0 V × 2.0 A = 4.0 W
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 W keeps an extra ½ when differentiating ½LI². 1.0 W is the stored energy ½LI² = 1.0 J at that instant, not its rate of increase. 8.0 W multiplies L by I² and dI/dt.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long air-cored solenoid is 50 cm long, has 1000 turns and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm², and carries a steady current of 2.0 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the energy stored in its magnetic field is about:

solution.concept: Self-inductance of a long solenoid L = µ₀N²A/l; energy U = ½LI²
solution.explanation: First find the self-inductance from the dimensions of the solenoid, then the energy for a current of 2.0 A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 mJ uses ½LI instead of ½LI². 10 mJ drops the ½. 1.3 mJ uses µ₀N²Al, putting the total number of turns N in place of n = N/l in L = µ₀n²Al.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each device or effect in List-I with the phenomenon on which it is based in List-II.

List-I:
A. Transformer
B. AC generator
C. Induction furnace
D. A spark across the switch when a circuit containing a large coil is suddenly broken

List-II:
I. Mutual induction
II. Self-induction
III. Heating by eddy currents
IV. Change of flux linkage of a coil rotated in a magnetic field

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Applications of electromagnetic induction
solution.explanation: A transformer transfers energy from the primary to the secondary through their mutual inductance. An AC generator produces an emf because the flux linkage of its rotating coil changes continuously. An induction furnace melts metal using the heat produced by large eddy currents. When a current in a coil of large self-inductance is cut off quickly, the large self-induced emf can make a spark jump across the switch.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap self- and mutual induction between the transformer and the spark, or attribute the generator to eddy currents; eddy currents are a loss in a generator, not its working principle.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance; mutual inductance; eddy currents; AC generator
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An ideal inductor, which has no resistance, limits the alternating current through it, although it lets a steady direct current pass without any opposition once the current has become steady.
Reason (R): The emf self-induced in the inductor opposes every change of current in it, giving it a reactance X_L = ωL, which is zero for a steady current (ω = 0).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL
solution.explanation: For an alternating current the current is always changing, so the self-induced emf L(di/dt) always opposes it; this opposition is the reactance ωL, which limits the rms current to V/(ωL). For a steady current di/dt = 0, the self-induced emf is zero and an ideal inductor offers no opposition. R gives exactly this reason.
solution.why_others_wrong: R is not a separate fact about inductors; the self-induced emf is the cause of the reactance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod of mass 0.10 kg lies across two smooth, horizontal, parallel conducting rails 0.40 m apart, which are joined at one end through a 1.0 Ω resistor; the rod and rails have negligible resistance. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T acts on the region. The rod is given a velocity of 2.0 m/s along the rails, away from the resistor, and is then left to itself. The total distance it moves before coming to rest is:

options.text: infinite, because the rod never stops completely

solution.concept: Motional emf, induced current and the retarding force; charge through the circuit = change of flux / R
solution.explanation: The induced current I = Blv/R gives a retarding force BIl. Over the whole motion, the impulse of this force equals the momentum lost: Bl × (total charge Q) = mv₀. The total charge is the change of flux divided by R: Q = BlX/R, where X is the distance moved.
steps: B²l²X/R = m v₀ → X = m v₀ R/(B²l²)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 m treats the initial retarding force as constant (uniform deceleration), though it falls as the rod slows. 10 m is twice the correct value. The speed decays exponentially, so the rod takes an infinite time to stop, but the distance covered is finite.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A metal rod slides with a constant speed of 2.0 m/s along two parallel conducting rails 0.50 m apart that are joined at one end, forming a rectangular circuit whose area grows as the rod moves away from the joined end. A uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the rails is increasing at a steady rate of 0.10 T/s. At the instant when the field is 0.50 T and the rod is 0.40 m from the joined end, the magnitude of the emf induced in the circuit is:

solution.concept: Faraday's law with both the field and the area changing: Φ = B l x, dΦ/dt = l x (dB/dt) + B l (dx/dt)
solution.explanation: Both changes increase the flux through the circuit (the area grows and the field grows), so their contributions add.
steps: Term from changing field: l x dB/dt = 0.50 × 0.40 × 0.10 = 0.02 V
Term from moving rod: B l v = 0.50 × 0.50 × 2.0 = 0.50 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 V keeps only the motional emf. 0.02 V keeps only the part due to the changing field. 0.48 V subtracts the two parts, although both increase the flux.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction; motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A coil of large inductance and small resistance is connected in series with a bulb across an AC supply of fixed voltage and frequency. A soft-iron rod is then pushed into the coil. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The self-inductance of the coil increases.
(b) The bulb becomes dimmer.
(c) The power factor of the circuit decreases.
(d) The current in the circuit starts to lead the supply voltage.
(e) If the same arrangement were connected to a steady DC supply instead, pushing the rod in would not change the steady brightness of the bulb.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL; impedance and power factor of an R–L circuit
solution.explanation: Soft iron has a large permeability, so the inductance of the coil increases (a). Then X_L = ωL increases, the impedance √(R² + X_L²) increases and the current falls, so the bulb dims (b). The power factor R/Z falls (c). In an R–L circuit the current always lags the voltage (d is false). With steady DC, an inductor offers no opposition once the current is steady, so the steady current depends only on the resistances (e).
steps: (d) false: current lags in an R–L circuit
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option containing (d) makes the inductive circuit capacitive. The options leaving out (c) or (a) miss the effect of the larger inductance on the power factor or the inductance itself.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor; power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flexible circular loop of wire lies in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The field is steadily increasing. Because of the current induced in it, the loop tends to:

options.text: rotate about one of its diameters
stay unchanged, since the net force on a closed loop in a uniform field is zero

solution.concept: Lenz's law; force on the induced current, F = I dl × B
solution.explanation: The induced current opposes the increase of the inward flux, so it produces an outward field inside the loop: it flows anticlockwise as seen by the reader. On each element the force I dl × B (dl anticlockwise, B into the page) points towards the centre. These inward forces squeeze the loop, tending to reduce its area and hence the flux, as Lenz's law requires.
steps: Inward flux increasing → induced current anticlockwise
F = I dl × B on each element points inwards
Loop tends to contract, reducing the flux
solution.why_others_wrong: Expansion would increase the flux, which is the opposite of what Lenz's law demands (it would happen if the field were decreasing). There is no torque about a diameter in a uniform field when the moment is along B. The net force is zero, but the inward forces on the different parts still tend to change the shape.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: contract (its area tends to decrease)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum predicted by Maxwell's equations is about:

solution.concept: Speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀)
solution.explanation: Maxwell found that his equations give waves travelling with speed 1/√(µ₀ε₀), which agrees with the measured speed of light.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.0 × 10¹⁶ m/s forgets the square root (it is c², in m² s⁻²). 3.3 × 10⁻⁹ m/s is √(µ₀ε₀), the reciprocal of c. 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁷ is µ₀ε₀ itself.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves: sources and nature

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each scientist in List-I with the contribution to the study of electromagnetic waves (List-II) that NCERT describes.

List-I:
A. J. C. Maxwell
B. H. Hertz
C. J. C. Bose
D. G. Marconi

List-II:
I. Transmitted electromagnetic waves over distances of many kilometres
II. Produced and observed electromagnetic waves of much shorter wavelength, 25 mm to 5 mm
III. Introduced the displacement current and predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves
IV. First demonstrated electromagnetic waves experimentally, in 1887

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: History of electromagnetic waves (NCERT introduction to the chapter)
solution.explanation: Maxwell added the displacement current to Ampere's law and showed that the equations predict electromagnetic waves. Hertz demonstrated such waves experimentally in 1887. J. C. Bose, working in Calcutta, produced and observed waves of much shorter wavelength (25 mm to 5 mm). Marconi transmitted electromagnetic waves over distances of many kilometres.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the theoretical prediction (Maxwell) with the first experiment (Hertz), or swap the short-wavelength work of Bose with Marconi's long-distance transmission.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', introduction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel-plate capacitor with circular plates of radius R is being charged by a steady current. Neglect edge effects, so that the uniform, changing electric field exists only in the cylindrical region between the plates. In the plane midway between the plates, the ratio of the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance R/2 from the axis to that at a distance 3R from the axis is:

solution.concept: Ampere–Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀ i_d, where i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt is the displacement current enclosed by the loop
solution.explanation: Take circular loops coaxial with the plates. The displacement current, equal to the charging current i, is spread uniformly over the plate area. A loop of radius r < R encloses the fraction r²/R² of it; a loop of radius r > R encloses all of it.
steps: r = 3R: B × 2π(3R) = µ₀ i → B = µ₀i/(6πR)
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 6 assumes B ∝ r at both points, as if the changing field filled the whole plane. 6 : 1 assumes B ∝ 1/r at both points, as if all of the displacement current were enclosed even at R/2. 2 : 3 inverts the answer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
